nameStory: The 'rattler' in this katydid's name comes from the distinctive rattling sound males make when they rub their wings together to attract mates. The 'round-winged' part refers to the notably rounded shape of their wing tips, which distinguishes them from their oblong-winged cousins. Think of it as nature's way of giving each species its own musical signature!
description: The Rattler Round-winged Katydid is a medium-sized green insect that looks like a musical leaf with legs. These katydids have broad, rounded wings that fold tent-like over their bodies, and long, thread-thin antennae that can be twice as long as their bodies. They're part of the grasshopper and cricket family (called Orthoptera), but unlike their ground-dwelling relatives, katydids are expert climbers who spend most of their time in trees and shrubs. Adult katydids typically measure about an inch to an inch and a half long.

idTips.label: Rounded Wing Tips
idTips.description: The wing tips are noticeably rounded rather than pointed or oval-shaped, giving them a softer, more circular appearance when folded over the back

idTips.label: Bright Green Color
idTips.description: Fresh leaf-green coloration that feels smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, though some individuals may have yellowish tinges

idTips.label: Long Thread Antennae
idTips.description: Extremely long, hair-thin antennae that constantly move and twitch, often extending far beyond the body length when extended forward

idTips.label: Distinctive Rattling Call
idTips.description: Males produce a rapid, buzzy rattling sound that's louder and more continuous than cricket chirps, especially noticeable on warm evenings

idTips.label: Leaf-like Body Shape
idTips.description: Flattened, oval body with wings that fold like a tent over the back, creating a leaf-mimicking silhouette when viewed from above

habitat: Rattler Round-winged Katydids prefer deciduous forests and woodland edges throughout New England, especially areas with oak, maple, and birch trees. They're commonly found in the shrub layer and lower tree canopy, about 3-15 feet off the ground, where they can easily blend in with the foliage. Look for them in parks, forest edges, and suburban areas with mature trees, particularly where there's a mix of sun and shade.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs laid the previous fall are developing in soil or leaf litter but won't hatch until late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most visible and vocal. Males call actively in evening hours, and both sexes can be found feeding on leaves in trees and shrubs.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, with mating and egg-laying occurring. Their green coloration provides excellent camouflage among changing leaves.
seasonality.winter: No adults present; the species overwinters as eggs in protected locations, waiting for spring warmth to begin the next generation's development.

funFact: Katydids have their ears located on their front legs, just below the 'knee' joint, allowing them to hear the mating calls of potential partners from surprisingly far distances - sometimes over 100 feet away!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Oblong-winged Katydid, but remember 'round vs. oblong' - if the wing tips look like they were trimmed with round scissors rather than cut straight across, you've got the Rattler Round-winged species. The Carinate Katydid is less common and has a more pronounced ridge down its back.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse katydids with grasshoppers - while both are in the same insect order, katydids are the 'tree dwellers' with longer antennae, while grasshoppers are the 'ground hoppers' with shorter, thicker antennae. The name 'katydid' comes from their call that sounds like 'Katy-did, Katy-didn't,' though this particular species sounds more like a rattle than the classic katydid chant.
compareHints: Compared to its Oblong-winged cousin, the Rattler Round-winged Katydid has distinctly rounded rather than elongated wing tips and typically produces a more continuous rattling call. The Carinate Katydid has a prominent ridge or 'keel' running down its back that the Round-winged species lacks. All three species share the same bright green coloration and tree-dwelling habits, but the wing shape is your best identifying feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its round-headed katydid relatives in New England, the oblong-winged katydid is distinguished by those characteristic elongated wings, while the rattler round-winged katydid has notably circular wings.
